notes:
I couldn't find any page where named Protestant traditions actually disagree over Numbers 9, and no Catholic, Orthodox or prosperity-teaching material on this chapter. What I did find is some disagreement over details, and a few differences in how teachers apply the text. Everything below comes from pages I read.

---

**v. 1**
- Wesley says verses 1–14 actually happened a month before the census in Numbers 1. Moses places them later because of the special case that came up afterwards. He adds that without this command Israel wouldn't have had to keep Passover at all until they reached Canaan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/9.htm
- Precept Austin quotes the NET Bible note: a full year has passed since the Exodus, and this second ruling on Passover would have come right after the tabernacle was consecrated. It also gives Ronald Allen's timeline: tabernacle set up on day 1 of month 1, tribal gifts on days 1–12, Levites set apart, Passover on day 14, census on day 1 of month 2, the make-up Passover on day 14 of month 2, departure on day 20 of month 2. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-9-commentary
- Bullinger likewise dates this command before the census. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/numbers-9.html

**v. 2**
- Matthew Henry says the first Passover was rushed. God wanted it kept again now that Israel was calmer and knew the law better, so their children would understand it more clearly. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_009.cfm
- Precept Austin points out that this would be Israel's last Passover for 38 years, until Joshua 5:10, because of the judgment in Numbers 14. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-9-commentary
- The Pulpit Commentary says Israel had been held at Sinai by God's direction (partly because of their own idolatry), and God did not want them to miss the comfort of Passover at its proper time. https://biblehub.com/numbers/9-2.htm
- Bible Hub's study notes link the verse to Christ: they quote Paul's words that Christ is our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7). https://biblehub.com/numbers/9-2.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik says Passover remembered the night God "passed over" homes marked with the lamb's blood. Christ fulfils it, and believers remember it at the Lord's Supper. He also quotes Wenham's guess that in the wilderness the blood may have been put on tents instead of doorposts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-9/

**vv. 4–5**
- Guzik notes that Numbers 1–10 shows almost no disobedience while Israel camped at Sinai. That makes their rebellion from chapter 11 onward all the more shocking. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-9/
- Bullinger counts this as the second of ten Passovers recorded in Scripture. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/numbers-9.html

**v. 6**
- Bullinger thinks the men were probably Mishael and Elizaphan, who had buried Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10:1-4); they were thus rendered unclean. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/numbers-9.html
- Guzik quotes Adam Clarke: the men were probably made unclean by helping bury someone, which was an act of necessity and mercy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-9/

**v. 7**
- Wesley frames their dilemma this way: skip the offering and be cut off, or keep it while unclean and also be cut off. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/9.htm
- Guzik sees two principles in tension: every Israelite had to take part, but no one ritually unclean could. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-9/
- Matthew Henry applies this to Christians: it should trouble us when something keeps us from worship or Communion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/9-13.htm

**v. 8**
- Guzik: God hadn't yet spoken on this case, so Moses had to ask him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-9/
- Henry: ministers should settle hard cases by asking God through his word and prayer, not by their own preferences. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/9-13.htm
- A sermon quoted by Precept Austin links this to James 1:5: if anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-9-commentary

**vv. 9–10**
- Wesley says Jewish teachers took these two cases as examples that cover similar obstacles, such as illness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/9.htm
- Gill reads "journey" as being in a distant country. Anyone travelling inside Israel had to come back for the feast. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/9-13.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch note that the Hebrew word for "distant" carries special scribal dots. The rabbis took this to mean distance from Jerusalem or the temple court. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/9-13.htm

**v. 11**
- Precept Austin: the only difference was the one-month delay. It quotes a sermon that calls the 30 days in between "days of grace" and a picture of God's plan of salvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-9-commentary
- Guzik, quoting Cole, says the make-up Passover was used historically under Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 30). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-9/
- Guzik also quotes Allen: Rabbi Gamaliel built on this verse his teaching that without the lamb, unleavened bread and bitter herbs, you haven't kept Passover. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-9/
- Bible Hub sees a "second chance" theme here and compares it to the late-hired workers in Matthew 20. https://biblehub.com/numbers/9.htm

**v. 12**
- Barnes: "all its statutes" means the rules about the lamb, not the whole feast. Jewish tradition says the "Little Passover" lasted only one day, and leaven didn't have to be removed from houses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/9-13.htm
- Henry: a delayed date doesn't mean any part of the ceremony can be cut short. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_009.cfm
- Guzik passes on three lessons from Spurgeon: feed on Christ, feed on all of Christ, and do it together with others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-9/

**v. 13** (what "cut off" means is disputed)
- Cambridge Bible: He shall suffer death by divine agency, not by punishment inflicted at the hands of the community. Ellicott also reads "bear his sin" as meaning death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/9-13.htm
- Gill leaves both options open: excommunication, or death directly from God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/9-13.htm
- Bridgeway says offenders were to be expelled from the camp. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/9-13.html
- Pulpit and Keil and Delitzsch say the threat was there to stop people using the make-up date as an excuse for their own convenience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/9-13.htm
- Clarke (a Methodist) applies it to the gospel: those who never "eat the true Passover" will be cut off from God's rest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/numbers-9.html
- Guzik: whoever refuses the lamb bears his own sin. He links this to John 6:53. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-9/

**v. 14**
- Wesley takes the "foreigner" to mean a proselyte, someone who had converted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/9.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch and Bridgeway both point to Exodus 12:48: a foreigner had to be circumcised first. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/9-13.htm
- Guzik, quoting Allen, sees God's purpose to reach all peoples here. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-9/

**v. 15**
- Wesley and Gill both say "Tent of the Testimony" means the part of the tabernacle that held the ark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/9.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/9-15.html
- Keil and Delitzsch reject a similar reading by some scholars on grammatical grounds. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/9-15.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the narrative jumps back to the day God took visible possession of his dwelling (Exodus 40:34). https://biblehub.com/numbers/9-15.htm
- Guzik: the cloud gave shade by day and the fire gave comfort at night. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-9/

**v. 16**
- Wesley and Henry: a cloud alone couldn't be seen at night, and fire alone could hardly be seen by day. God showed he kept them night and day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/9.htm
- Henry also suggests the cloud and fire stood for the darkness and terror of the Old Testament era, compared with the clearer revelation in Christ. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_009.cfm
- Pulpit: unlike the glory that filled the tent for a moment, this sign was not passing. https://biblehub.com/numbers/9-16.htm

**v. 17**
- Wesley and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say "lifted" means the cloud rose higher, so the whole camp could see it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/9-18.htm

**v. 18** (did God speak aloud?)
- Gill: there was no audible voice. The cloud's movement itself counted as God's command. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/9-18.htm
- The Cambridge Bible disagrees: Not only was a sign given by the cloud, but Jehovah used to give an oral command to Moses when the march was to begin and end. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/9-18.htm
- Henry's Concise Commentary (an older Dissenter) warns that when people's minds already lean toward a doubtful plan, what they call "the moving of the cloud" is generally no more than a temptation Satan is permitted to propose. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/9-18.htm

**v. 19**
- Wesley: "the LORD's charge" means God's command to stay as long as the cloud stayed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/9.htm
- Henry: no doubt they longed to press on, but He that believeth doth not make haste. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_009.cfm
- The Treasury of Scripture Knowledge, quoted by Precept Austin: no time is wasted while waiting for God's time. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-9-commentary

**vv. 20–22**
- Wesley says the point is repeated because it was a constant miracle. Using Isaiah 63:14, he says the cloud's guidance stands for the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and he turns it into a prayer of surrender. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/9.htm
- Guzik: the cloud was unpredictable, so Israel couldn't run on routine. He applies it with Colossians 3:15: let God's peace act as the umpire in your heart. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-9/
- G. Campbell Morgan (quoted by Precept Austin) says we no longer have a visible guide. We know God's guidance through ongoing fellowship with the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-9-commentary

**v. 23**
- Precept Austin: "command" is a key word in the chapter, and every time it appears Israel obeys. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-9-commentary
- Constable says the writer stresses Israel's obedience, saying it seven times. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/9-15.html
- Henry: with the cloud as guide, Israel didn't need war councils, spies or scouts. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_009.cfm

---

**Differences between traditions:** Besides the disputes in v. 13 and v. 18, the only contrast is in how teachers apply the cloud today:
- **Wesley (Methodist founder):** the cloud as a picture of the Spirit's guidance.
- **Henry:** a warning against claiming "the cloud moved" to back your own wishes.
- **Guzik:** God's peace as the inner guide.

I found nothing from Lutheran, Reformed, Pentecostal or Anglican teachers specifically on this chapter.

**Other views:**
- **Modern scholarship:** only the NET Bible notes quoted on Precept Austin (dating, and that the meaning of the word *pesach* is uncertain).
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** nothing on this chapter. The Haydock (Catholic) commentary is listed on Bible Hub, but I didn't read it.
- **Prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching:** nothing found.

My search budget ran out before I could read the Haydock, Gill and Pulpit pages for the whole chapter, so those gaps may be fillable.
